A hot source, a thin hydrogen cloud, three lines of sight: what does each spectrum show?

Listen to the intro

About: Kirchhoff's three spectra from one gas: the intensity is drawn towards the source function S = B(Tgas)

About this simulation

On screen
Left: a 6000 K source disc and a thin hydrogen cloud whose dashed outline takes the blackbody colour of the gas. Three lines of sight run to three strips from 400 to 700 nm: the source directly, the source through the gas, and the gas alone against empty sky. Each strip is labelled with the kind of spectrum it shows now. Right: the intensity at the centre of the red line against the optical depth, with S dashed.
Controls
Gas temperature sets the temperature of the cloud, 5000 to 7000 K; the source stays at 6000 K. Line optical depth τ0 sets how opaque the gas is at the centres of its four lines, 0 to 5; between the lines it is transparent. The Readouts panel below the controls gives S and the two intensities at the red line.
Measured
S and the intensities are line-centre values at 656.28 nm divided by the source's intensity there, from I = I0 e−τ + S(1 − e−τ). Strip brightness is on one fixed scale, 0 to 2.5 × the source. In the top two strips brightness grows in proportion to the intensity, so dark lines show at their true depth, and a white trace over the middle strip plots I(λ) on the same scale, with the source's level dashed; in the gas-alone strip it grows as the square root of the intensity, so that faint emission lines stay visible.
Assumptions
The source is a 6000 K blackbody. The gas is a uniform slab at one temperature in local thermodynamic equilibrium, so its source function is the Planck function, S = B(Tgas): this is what lets the line colour depend only on Tgas against the source. Scattering is neglected. The gas absorbs only in four hydrogen Balmer lines (656, 486, 434 and 410 nm), each a Gaussian 4 nm wide; between them it is transparent. All four are given the same centre optical depth τ0 for clarity; in real hydrogen Hα is by far the strongest, and Hβ, Hγ and Hδ are only about 14, 5 and 2 per cent as opaque at their centres.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Cool gas in front

Set the gas temperature to 5000 K and the optical depth to 0, so that the gas is transparent, the middle strip matches the top one and the bottom strip is dark. Before you raise the optical depth, predict what the middle and bottom strips will show when it reaches 1. Then raise it to 1.

2 · Gas as hot as the source

Keep the optical depth at 1. Before you move the gas temperature, predict what the middle strip will show when the gas is exactly as hot as the source, at 6000 K. Then raise the gas temperature to 6000 K.

3 · Gas hotter than the source

Keep the optical depth at 1. Before you move the gas temperature, predict what the middle strip will show when the gas is hotter than the source, at 7000 K. Then raise the gas temperature to 7000 K.

4 · Doubling a thin layer

Set the gas temperature to 5000 K and the optical depth to 0.1. The readout gives the intensity at the centre of the red line through the gas as 0.95, a shallow dip of 0.05 below the source. Before you move the optical depth, predict the intensity there when the optical depth is doubled to 0.2. Then set it to 0.2.

5 · A thick layer of gas

Keep the gas temperature at 5000 K. Before you move the optical depth, predict how the intensities at the centre of the red line through the gas and from the gas alone compare when the optical depth is 5. Then raise it to 5.

6 · What you found

One rule makes all three spectra. At the wavelengths of its lines the gas drives the intensity towards its source function S = B(Tgas): I = I0e−τ + S(1 − e−τ).

Gas cooler than the light behind it (S below it) gives dark absorption lines; gas hotter than it, or seen against empty sky, gives bright emission lines; at equal temperature the lines vanish.

Gas thick enough at every wavelength shows only S, whatever lies behind: that is why a hot, dense body gives a continuous spectrum.

The Physics

Three Spectra from One Gas · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A spectrum can be continuous, crossed by dark lines, or made of bright lines. This sim views one thin hydrogen gas in front of a 6000 K source along three lines of sight, and lets you change the gas to find what decides the kind of spectrum.

What you'll learn

  • What a layer of gas does to the light that passes through it.
  • How the gas temperature Tgas sets the look of its lines.
  • How the line optical depth τ0 sets how much the gas matters.
  • What the source function S measures.
The setup: a source, a thin gas cloud (dashed) and three lines of sight, each ending on a spectrum strip.

What's on screen

  • Source disc, 6000 K, and dashed gas cloud, outlined in the colour of a blackbody at Tgas.
  • Three strips, 400 to 700 nm: the source directly, through the gas, and the gas alone against empty sky.
  • White trace over the middle strip: I(λ), with the source's level dashed.
  • Inset and Readouts: the red-line (656.28 nm) intensity against τ0, with its numbers.

Fixed: the source is 6000 K, each line is a Gaussian 4 nm wide, and the gas is one uniform slab with no scattering. All four lines share one centre optical depth τ0, a simplification: in real hydrogen Hβ, Hγ and Hδ are only about 14, 5 and 2 per cent as opaque as Hα.

03

The gas pulls the intensity towards its source function S

At the wavelengths of its lines the gas absorbs light and also emits its own. For a uniform slab of optical depth τ, the notes (3.29) put the two together:

Equation (3.29). I0 is the intensity entering the gas, S its source function, and I the intensity that leaves.

At τ = 0, I = I0. As τ grows, I moves towards S, whichever side of S it starts on. Here τ is τ0 at a line centre, and nearly zero between the lines. The sim measures every intensity in units of the source's intensity at the same wavelength, so I0 = 1 on the middle line of sight and 0 on the bottom one.

I against τ at 5000 K, like the notes’ Figure 32. Both curves approach S.
Key idea. One equation covers all three strips. Only the light entering the gas, I0, differs between them.
See itSet the gas to 5000 K with τ0 = 1. Watch for: the middle strip dipping to 0.67 at the lines while the bottom strip rises to 0.30 at the same wavelengths.
04

Dark when cooler, bright when hotter: S compared with the light behind

In local thermodynamic equilibrium a gas's source function is the Planck function at its own temperature (Kirchhoff's law, notes 3.31):

Equation (3.31). The sim uses S = B(Tgas) / B(6000 K) at each wavelength.

B rises with temperature at every wavelength, so S is below 1 for a gas cooler than the source and above 1 for a hotter one.

  • Cooler: I is pulled below the source on the middle line of sight (dark lines) and up from 0 on the bottom one (bright lines).
  • Equal: S = 1 at every wavelength, so the middle strip matches the top one. The bottom strip still shows bright lines.
  • Hotter: I is pulled above the source, so the lines are bright on the continuum.
S at the red line: 0.47 at 5000 K, 1.00 at 6000 K, 1.72 at 7000 K.
Tgas τ0

See itHeat the gas further, to 7000 K. Watch for: bright lines standing above the continuum in the middle strip, at the same four wavelengths.
05

Thin layer, thick layer: the change grows with τ0 until I reaches S

For a thin layer, e−τ ≈ 1 − τ, and (3.29) becomes (notes 3.30):

Equation (3.30), for τ ≪ 1. The change from I0 is proportional to τ, and largest at the line centres.

At 5000 K on the middle line of sight, I0 = 1 and S = 0.47. The red line reads 0.95 at τ0 = 0.1, and 0.90 at 0.2. The dip is nearly doubled (0.050 to 0.095): only nearly, because e−τ is only approximately 1 − τ.

A thick layer is different. At τ0 = 5, e−τ is below 0.01, so the light that entered is lost and I = S. Through the gas the red line reads 0.48, and from the gas alone 0.47. A body that is optically thick shows only S (notes, 3.3).

Key idea. How far I gets towards S is set by τ. Where it ends up is set by S.
See itDouble a thin layer: τ0 from 0.1 to 0.2 at 5000 K. Watch for: I through the gas falling from 0.95 to 0.90.
See itNow raise τ0 to 5. Watch for: both curves in the inset reaching the dashed S line, and the two readouts nearly equal.
06

Where it matters

  • Stellar spectra. Light from hot layers passes through cooler gas above them, so almost every star shows dark lines on a continuum: the Fraunhofer lines of the Sun (Kirchhoff's third law, notes 3.1).
  • Glowing gas. A hot gas of low density seen against an empty background gives only bright lines, at the wavelengths of its atoms (second law).
  • Dense, hot bodies. A body that is optically thick at every wavelength gives I = S, a continuous spectrum (first law).

The sim's rule S = B(Tgas) holds for gas in local thermodynamic equilibrium. The notes do not treat gas out of it, such as the thinnest outer layers of a star.

07

Summary

In one line. A gas changes the light that passes through it, and one equation, with the gas's temperature and optical depth as inputs, decides which kind of spectrum results.

Key points

  • I moves from I0 towards S as τ grows.
  • In equilibrium S = B(Tgas), set by the gas alone.
  • Lines are dark if S is below I0, bright if above, and absent if equal.
  • A thin layer changes I by (S − I0)τ; a thick one gives I = S.

Common mix-ups

  • "A cool gas cannot glow." At 5000 K and τ0 = 1, the gas alone gives 0.30 of the source at the red line.
  • "Gas in front always makes dark lines." Only when S is below the light behind. At 7000 K the lines are bright.
  • "A thick layer drives I to zero." It drives I to S, from above or from below.

Things to try on your own

  • With τ0 = 1, sweep Tgas from 5000 to 7000 K. Find where the middle strip's lines vanish.
  • At Tgas = 7000 K, raise τ0 from 0 to 5.
